paragraphs: In the book Animal Farm by George Orwell there is a big theme about how power corrupts people or in this case animals. At first the animals want to be free from Mr. Jones because he is mean but then the pigs take over and they become even worse then he was. I am going to show how Napoleon changes and how the power goes to his head throughout the story so you can see how the farm fails.

Then later in the book things get way worse because Napoleon chases Snowball away with his dogs. Another thing is that the commandments start changing on the wall but the animals are to dumb to notice mostly and they just believe whatever they are told. Also Napoleon changes a lot because he starts acting like a human which they said they would never do at the beginning. By the end he is wearing clothes and carrying a whip and the commandment says "All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others." This is a famous quote that shows the theme of corruption because it doesnt make sense and it just gives the pigs more power to do whatever they want. Napoleon is not even a comrade anymore he is just a boss who treats the other animals like slaves while he lives in the big house.

In conclusion the book shows that power makes people act bad and Napoleon is the best example of this. He started as a pig who wanted freedom but he ended up being just like Mr. Jones or even worse in the end. The ending where the animals look from pig to man and cant tell the difference is really sad because it shows nothing really changed. In George Orwell’s Animal Farm, the dream of a fair society quickly turns into a nightmare as the leaders become obsessed with control. The book shows how even the best intentions can be ruined by greed and the desire for authority. The main theme of the novel is that power corrupts those who hold it, eventually making them exactly like the oppressors they fought to replace. This transition is best seen through Napoleon, a pig who starts as a revolutionary but ends up as a cruel dictator.

At the start of the book, the animals believe in "Animalism," which is based on the idea that all animals are equal and humans are the enemy. However, almost immediately after the rebellion, Napoleon starts to take more than his fair share. When the milk and apples go missing, Squealer explains that they are needed for the pigs' health, and the animals are told to agree for the good of the farm. This is the first sign that the leaders are putting themselves above everyone else. Even though the original goal was equality, the pigs already started thinking they were more important than the other animals.

As the story moves forward, Napoleon uses fear to keep his power. He gets rid of his rival, Snowball, by using his trained dogs to chase him away. After this, he stops all debates and makes all the decisions himself. The character Boxer shows how the other animals deal with this by saying, "Napoleon is always right." This quotation shows how Napoleon has successfully manipulated the animals into giving up their own voices. By using a mix of violence and propaganda, Napoleon moves from being a leader to a ruler who cannot be questioned.

By the end of the novel, the corruption is complete, and Napoleon has changed into a mirror image of Mr. Jones. The pigs start living in the farmhouse, sleeping in beds, and even drinking alcohol, which were all things they originally banned. The most famous quote in the book shows this change: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This shows that the original meaning of equality has been totally destroyed. Napoleon even starts walking on two legs and carrying a whip, proving that he has become the very thing he once hated.

In conclusion, Animal Farm is a warning about how easily power can be abused. Through the character of Napoleon, George Orwell shows that when people or animals get too much control, they often lose sight of their original goals. The farm started with a dream of freedom, but it ended with a new kind of slavery because the leaders refused to share power. The book proves that without checks and balances, any rebellion can lead back to the same problems it was trying to solve.

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, the story starts with a dream of equality, but it quickly turns into a nightmare. The most important theme in the book is how power corrupts those who have it. At the beginning, the animals just want to be free from Mr. Jones, but by the end, the pigs are just as bad as the humans were. This development is mostly seen through the character of Napoleon, who goes from being a quiet leader to a scary dictator. The book shows that when leaders get too much power without any rules to stop them, they will always end up hurting the people they are supposed to help.

After the Rebellion, the animals are supposed to be equal, but the pigs immediately start taking more for themselves. They claim they need better food because they are the brainworkers of the farm. When the other animals find out the pigs are taking the milk and apples, Squealer explains that "It is for your sake that we drink that milk and eat those apples." This shows the beginning of corruption because the pigs are already putting their needs above everyone else's. Even though Napoleon isn't the one talking yet, he is part of this group that thinks they deserve more just because they are smart and can manipulate the others.

Napoleon's change becomes more obvious when he decides to get rid of Snowball so he can have total control. Instead of using words or debates, he uses force by training a group of dogs to attack his rival. After Snowball is gone, Napoleon cancels the Sunday meetings and decides that all decisions will be made by a committee of pigs. The book says that "Napoleon was a large, rather fierce-looking Berkshire boar... with a reputation for getting his own way." This quote shows that he was always looking for power, and once he got it, he used fear to keep it. By removing the animals' right to vote, he moves from a leader to a boss who doesn't have to answer to anyone.

As the story goes on, Napoleon starts breaking the Seven Commandments that the animals wrote at the start. He moves into the farmhouse, drinks alcohol, and even starts killing other animals who disagree with him. The most famous change is when the commandment "All animals are equal" is changed to "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This shows that the original goal of the Rebellion is completely dead. Napoleon has become so corrupted by his power that he does not even pretend to care about equality anymore. He uses his power to make himself a king while the other animals suffer and starve.

In the end, the corruption is complete when the pigs start walking on two legs and wearing clothes. The other animals look through the window and realize they cannot tell the difference between the pigs and the humans. The novel says, "The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig... but already it was impossible to say which was which." This final scene proves the theme that power corrupts absolutely. Napoleon's journey from a rebel pig to a human-like tyrant shows that once someone gets enough power, they will eventually become the very thing they fought against in the first place.

In the book Animal Farm by George Orwell, there is a big theme about how power corrupts people. This happens when the animals take over the farm from Mr. Jones because they want a better life. Napoleon is the main character who shows this. He starts as a normal pig but then he becomes a leader and changes everything. This essay will show how power makes him bad and how the farm changes from the beginning to the end.

At the start of the book, the animals all want to be equal. Old Major gives a big speech and they write the Seven Commandments on the barn wall. One of them says "All animals are equal" (Orwell 24). This shows that everyone was supposed to be the same at the beginning of the revolution. Napoleon was just one of the pigs then and he didn't have all the power yet. This part of the book is about everyone working together for a good cause.

As the story goes on, Napoleon starts to want more power for himself. He gets rid of Snowball using the dogs he trained in secret. After that, the animals have to do whatever he says and they don't get to vote anymore. Squealer tells everyone "Napoleon is always right" (Orwell 56). This shows Napoleon is becoming a leader who doesn't listen to others. He is changing from a pig who followed Old Major’s ideas into a boss who just wants to be in charge of everything on the farm.

By the end of the book, Napoleon and the other pigs are basically acting like humans. They start drinking alcohol and sleeping in beds even though the rules said they shouldn't. The sheep even start saying "Four legs good, two legs better" (Orwell 134). This shows the pigs think they are better than the other animals now. Napoleon is wearing clothes and carrying a whip which is really different from how he was at the start. He isn't even like the other animals anymore because he has too much power and became a human.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that power makes people act differently and usually in a bad way. Napoleon started out wanting a revolution but he ended up being just like Mr. Jones. This happens in real life too when people get too much control over others. The theme of power corrupting is really important because it shows that even if you start with good ideas, you can still end up being a mean leader if you don't have anyone to stop you.

In the novel Animal Farm by George Orwell, the most important theme is how power corrupts those who have it. At the start, the animals have a dream of a world where they are free from human cruelty. However, as the pigs take control of the farm, they start to act exactly like the humans they overthrew. This essay will show how Napoleon’s rise to power turns a revolution for equality into a terrifying dictatorship where "All animals are equal" is no longer the truth.

At the beginning of the book, the idea of Animalism is based on the equality of all animals. After Old Major dies, Napoleon and Snowball lead the revolution, but Napoleon already shows signs of wanting more power than the others. When the Seven Commandments are first written on the barn wall, the final rule is "All animals are equal." This shows that the original goal was a fair society where everyone shared the work and the rewards. Napoleon’s changes start small, like when he takes the milk and apples for the pigs, but it is the first sign that he believes the pigs are more important than the other animals.

As the story progresses, Napoleon uses fear to consolidate his power and get rid of his competition. The most significant change happens when Napoleon uses his secret dogs to chase Snowball off the farm. Without Snowball to argue for different ideas, Napoleon becomes the sole leader. Orwell writes that "the animals listened first to Napoleon, then to Snowball, and could not make up their minds which was right," which shows they were still trying to be democratic. However, once Napoleon takes over by force, he stops the Sunday meetings and begins making all the decisions himself, showing that his power is no longer coming from the animals' consent but from his own strength.

Napoleon’s character continues to change until he is a complete tyrant who manipulates the rules to benefit himself. For example, when the pigs start sleeping in the farmhouse beds, the other animals are confused because they remember a rule against it. Squealer, acting on Napoleon's orders, changes the commandment to read, "No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets." This shows how Napoleon uses his power to rewrite history and the law so he can live in luxury while others suffer. By the end of the book, Napoleon is even wearing clothes and carrying a whip, proving that he has become exactly what he once hated because power has totally changed his personality.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that even the best intentions can be ruined by the desire for power. Napoleon starts as a rebel leader but ends up as a cruel dictator who is indistinguishable from a human. The final version of the commandments, "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others," perfectly sums up the corruption of the revolution. Orwell’s message is clear: when leaders get absolute power and are not held accountable, they will eventually use it to benefit themselves at the expense of everyone else.

In George Orwell’s novel Animal Farm, the most important theme is how power can corrupt even the best intentions. At the start of the book, the animals want freedom and equality for everyone. However, as the pigs take control, they slowly change into the same kind of leaders they once hated. This transformation is seen mostly through Napoleon, who starts as a leader of the rebellion but eventually turns into a tyrant. By looking at how Napoleon changes and how the rules of the farm shift, it becomes clear that power is a dangerous tool that usually leads to corruption and inequality.

At the beginning, the pigs are seen as the natural leaders because of their intelligence. After Old Major dies, Napoleon and Snowball take over to organize the rebellion based on the idea of Animalism. Orwell writes, "The work of teaching and organizing the others fell naturally upon the pigs, who were generally recognized as being the cleverest of the animals." This shows that in the beginning, the pigs used their skills to help the farm. However, this also created a small gap between the pigs and the other animals. Because they were seen as the cleverest, they were able to start taking more control without the other animals questioning them, which is the first step toward the corruption of their power.

As the story continues, Napoleon uses force to make sure he has all the power for himself. He stops caring about the common good and starts caring about his own authority. When he chases Snowball away with his dogs, he changes the way the farm is run by getting rid of the Sunday meetings where everyone had a vote. Orwell describes a scene where "Napoleon, with the dogs following him, now mounted on to the raised portion of the floor where Major had previously stood to deliver his speech." This quotation shows how Napoleon is physically and symbolically putting himself above the other animals. By using the dogs to scare everyone, he moves from being a leader who listens to a dictator who rules by fear.

By the end of the novel, the corruption of the pigs is complete, and they are basically humans. Napoleon starts wearing clothes, drinking alcohol, and carrying a whip. The original Seven Commandments are replaced by just one sentence: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This quotation is the ultimate proof of how much the theme of power has developed. It shows that the pigs no longer care about the original goal of the revolution, which was equality. They have used their power to rewrite the rules so they can stay in charge and live in luxury while the other animals work and suffer.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that power is a dangerous thing that can change people for the worse. Napoleon’s journey from a revolutionary pig to a human-like dictator proves that once a group gets a taste of control, they often do anything to keep it. The way the commandments were changed shows that the pigs completely abandoned their friends for their own benefit. Orwell’s message is clear: if people do not stay alert and hold leaders accountable, those in power will eventually use it to take away the freedom of others, making the new system just as bad as the old one.

In the novel Animal Farm by George Orwell, the most important theme is how power corrupts those who possess it. At first, the animals want to create a fair society where everyone is equal and free from human cruelty. However, as the pigs take control, they slowly turn into the very thing they hated. Napoleon, the main antagonist, shows this change most clearly. His journey from a quiet leader to a cruel dictator proves the idea that power leads to a loss of morality. Through Napoleon's transformation, Orwell shows that even a rebellion with good intentions can fail if those in charge care more about themselves than the common good.

In the beginning, the animals are unified by the dream of Old Major, who says, "All animals are equal." This promise of equality is what motivates the rebellion against Mr. Jones. However, even early on, Napoleon starts to show signs of greed. When the cows are milked, the milk disappears, and it is later revealed that the pigs are keeping it for themselves. Squealer justifies this by saying the pigs need it for their "brainwork." This is the first step in the pigs seeing themselves as better than the others, showing that power is already starting to change their priorities and making them feel entitled to special treatment.

As the story progresses, Napoleon uses fear to solidify his control and get rid of his rival, Snowball. He raises a pack of dogs to chase Snowball away and then takes over all the decision-making. Instead of having debates, Napoleon decides everything himself. Boxer, the horse, starts saying, "Napoleon is always right," which shows how the animals have stopped thinking for themselves and have given Napoleon total power. This shift allows Napoleon to change the rules of the farm without anyone questioning him, leading to more corruption and the betrayal of the original goals of the rebellion. By removing all opposition, Napoleon ensures that his power is absolute.

By the middle of the book, Napoleon’s corruption becomes violent. He uses the dogs to execute animals who he claims are traitors to make sure no one ever speaks up again. The Seven Commandments, which were meant to be unchangeable laws, are secretly altered to fit Napoleon’s desires. For example, when he starts killing animals, the commandment "No animal shall kill any other animal" is changed to "No animal shall kill any other animal without cause." This shows that Napoleon is no longer interested in justice; he only cares about maintaining his own authority and using his power to bypass the rules he helped create.

At the end of the novel, the corruption is complete when the pigs begin walking on two legs and carrying whips. The most famous commandment is changed to the ultimate contradiction: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This quote perfectly illustrates how the original dream of equality has been destroyed by the pigs' hunger for status. In the final scene, when the pigs are playing cards with humans, the other animals realize they cannot tell the difference between the pigs and the men. Napoleon has become exactly like Mr. Jones, proving that the gain of power has fully corrupted his character and the entire revolution.

In George Orwell's novella Animal Farm, the story serves as a cautionary tale about how leadership can easily turn into a dictatorship. The most important theme in the book is how power corrupts those who hold it, eventually leading them to become exactly like the oppressors they fought against. Through the character of Napoleon, the reader sees how the original goal of animal equality is slowly destroyed by greed and the desire for control. Napoleon’s transformation from a quiet pig into a ruthless tyrant shows that when individuals gain absolute power, they often do anything to keep it.

At the beginning of the story, the animals are inspired by Old Major’s vision of a world where "all animals are brothers." However, as soon as the Rebellion is over, Napoleon starts to show signs that he cares more about his own group than the other animals. One of the first signs of his corruption is when the cows' milk goes missing. It is later revealed that the pigs took it for themselves. When the other animals question this, the pigs use Squealer to justify it, saying they need it for their "brainwork." This moment is important because it shows that Napoleon is already starting to prioritize his own needs. As the book says, "The milk had disappeared," which marks the start of the pigs taking special privileges and moving away from equality.

As the story progresses into the middle, Napoleon uses fear and violence to consolidate his power and remove any competition. He raises a pack of dogs to be his private police force and uses them to chase Snowball off the farm. Once his main rival is gone, Napoleon stops holding meetings and begins making all the decisions himself. He even uses Boxer’s loyalty to solidify his control, leading Boxer to adopt the maxim, "Napoleon is always right." This shows how Napoleon has successfully manipulated the animals into believing that he is the only one capable of leading, even though he is actually taking away their freedom and making them work harder than ever before.

By the end of the novel, the corruption of Napoleon and the pigs is complete, and they have become indistinguishable from the humans they once hated. They begin walking on two legs, wearing clothes, and drinking alcohol, which were all things forbidden by the original Seven Commandments. The most shocking change occurs when the commandments are replaced by a single sentence: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This quotation perfectly illustrates the theme of corruption because it shows that the idea of equality has been twisted to justify the pigs' superior status. Napoleon has fully abandoned the revolution's goals to become a human-like dictator who treats the animals just as badly as Mr. Jones did.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that power is a dangerous thing that can change even the most well-meaning movements into systems of oppression. Napoleon’s journey from a revolutionary pig to a cruel leader proves that absolute power corrupts those who wield it. By looking at how he used the milk, the dogs, and eventually changed the laws of the farm, it is clear that he valued his own authority over the well-being of his fellow animals. Orwell uses this transformation to warn readers that without accountability, those in charge will always find ways to put themselves above everyone else.

In the novel Animal Farm by George Orwell, language is just as powerful as physical force when it comes to maintaining control over a group. The pigs, who are the smartest animals on the farm, use their ability to read and write to manipulate the other animals and secure their own power. Squealer, the pig who acts as Napoleon’s spokesperson, is the main character who demonstrates this theme through his constant use of rhetoric and propaganda. By rewriting the Seven Commandments and changing the history of the farm, the pigs show that whoever controls the language also controls the truth. This essay will trace how the use of language evolves from a tool of liberation into a tool of total oppression.

At the beginning of the story, language is used to unite the animals against their human oppressor, Mr. Jones. After the rebellion, the animals create the Seven Commandments to ensure that everyone remains equal. The most important rule is the last one, which states, "All animals are equal" (Orwell 24). At first, this simple sentence provides a clear vision for the future and gives the animals a sense of purpose. However, the pigs quickly realize that because the other animals cannot read well, they can use their literacy to interpret the laws however they want. This shows that even a good message can be used for control if only a small group of people are allowed to define what the words mean.

As the pigs start taking more control and enjoying human luxuries, Squealer’s character becomes essential to the theme of manipulation. Every time the pigs break one of the original rules, Squealer secretly changes the written Commandments on the barn wall to justify their behavior. For example, when the pigs move into the farmhouse, the animals remember a rule against sleeping in beds. Squealer changes the wall to read, "No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets" (Orwell 67). He explains to the confused animals that the rule was never against beds, but only against the human invention of sheets. By adding just two words, Squealer uses language to redefine reality and makes the animals doubt their own memories, which allows the pigs to get away with anything.

Furthermore, the pigs use language to rewrite history, turning the farm’s past into a weapon for Napoleon. Even though Snowball was a hero at the Battle of the Cowshed, Squealer begins telling the animals that Snowball was actually "in league with Jones" from the very beginning (Orwell 79). When the animals try to remember Snowball’s bravery, Squealer uses complicated words and fake statistics to confuse them until they accept his version of events. This change in Squealer shows how language can be used to isolate individuals and make the truth completely subjective. Because the animals cannot articulate their own thoughts as well as Squealer can, they eventually stop questioning the pigs and accept Napoleon’s version of history as the only truth.

By the end of the novel, the manipulation of language is complete, and the pigs have become the very thing they once hated. All the original Seven Commandments are painted over and replaced with a single, contradictory statement: "ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS" (Orwell 134). This sentence is the ultimate example of how language can be used to control others because it makes no logical sense, yet the animals are too intimidated to challenge it. Through Squealer’s constant lying and the gradual corruption of the farm’s laws, Orwell proves that literacy and the control of information are the most important tools of a dictator. In conclusion, the abuse of language in Animal Farm shows that without the ability to think critically and speak for themselves, people will always be at the mercy of those who use words to hide the truth.

Animal Farm is a book about animals who take over a farm because they are tired of Farmer Jones and his rules. This develops the theme because power makes him use the dogs for scary things. He changes from a normal pig who wants to help to a leader who just wants to chase people away from the farm.

Later in the story, the pigs start acting like humans more and more. The book says, "The pigs suddenly moved into the farmhouse and took up their residence there." This quote shows that the pigs liked the house because it had a lot of room for them to sit down. Napoleon changes here because he stops sleeping outside and starts using a bed. This proves that power is corrupt because he is not following the old rules anymore and he is becoming just like Farmer Jones who he used to hate when the book first started.

In George Orwell's novel Animal Farm, the dream of equality quickly turns into a nightmare as leadership shifts from liberation to tyranny. The most important theme in the book is how power corrupts those who hold it. At the beginning, the animals just want to be free from Mr. Jones and his cruelty, but as the pigs take control, they become exactly like the humans they once hated. Through the character of Napoleon, Orwell shows that even a revolution with good intentions can fail if the leaders care more about power than the people they are supposed to represent.

At the start of the story, the animals are inspired by Old Major’s vision of a world where "all animals are equal." After the rebellion, Napoleon is just one of many pigs helping to organize the farm. However, he quickly shows that he is more interested in control than cooperation. While Snowball wants to build a windmill to help everyone, Napoleon focuses on training the puppies in secret. Orwell describes Napoleon as "not much of a talker, but with a reputation for getting his own way." This shows that even early on, Napoleon was looking for ways to gain authority rather than working for the common good.

As the story progresses, Napoleon’s need for power leads him to use violence and manipulation. The biggest turning point is when he uses his trained dogs to chase Snowball off the farm. Once Snowball is gone, Napoleon takes away the animals' right to vote and starts making all the decisions himself. He also starts changing the Seven Commandments to fit his own needs. For example, when the pigs start sleeping in beds, the commandment is changed to "No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets." This illustrates how Napoleon uses his power to rewrite the rules so he can live a life of luxury while the other animals suffer.

By the end of the novel, Napoleon’s corruption is complete, and he has become a total dictator. He no longer hides his desire to be like a human. He starts wearing clothes, drinking alcohol, and carrying a whip. The ultimate betrayal happens when the Seven Commandments are replaced by a single sentence: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This quote is famous because it shows how the pigs have completely destroyed the original goal of the revolution. Napoleon’s transition from a quiet leader to a tyrant shows that having absolute power made him lose his connection to the other animals.

In conclusion, Animal Farm serves as a warning about how power can change a person for the worse. Napoleon’s journey from a revolutionary pig to a human-like dictator proves that without checks and balances, leaders will often put their own interests first. By the time the animals look through the window and cannot tell the difference between the pigs and the humans, it is clear that the revolution has failed. Orwell’s message is that power does not just change the way a society is run; it changes the very nature of those who possess it.

In the book Animal Farm by George Orwell, there is a big theme about how power can make people, or in this case animals, act really bad. At the start of the book, everyone wants to be the same and have a good life without humans. But as the story goes on, the pigs start to take over everything. Napoleon is the main character who shows this because he starts out as a leader for the rebellion but ends up being just like a mean human. This essay will show how power corrupts the animals and makes them forget their original goals.

At the beginning of the book, things were supposed to be fair for everyone. Old Major had a dream where animals were free. After the rebellion, they wrote down seven commandments on the wall to keep things equal. One of the most important things they said was "All animals are equal" (Orwell 24). This quote shows that they really believed they were going to have a perfect world where no one was the boss of anyone else. Napoleon was there and he seemed like he was going along with it, but you could tell he wanted more power even then.

As time went on, Napoleon started to change and he really wanted to be the only leader. He did not like Snowball at all, so he used his big scary dogs to chase him right off the farm. This was a huge turning point because it showed Napoleon was using fear to get what he wanted. Instead of talking about things, he just used force. He also started taking the best stuff for the pigs, like the milk and apples. When the other animals complained, Squealer would just tell them the pigs needed it for their brains. This shows how Napoleon was using his power to get treats while everyone else worked hard.

Towards the end of the book, Napoleon does not even act like an animal anymore. He starts living in the house and sleeping in a bed, which was against the rules they made. He changed the commandments on the wall so he would not get in trouble for breaking them. One quote that is really important is when the wall says "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others" (Orwell 134). This shows that the theme of power corrupting is totally finished because Napoleon has made himself the king. He is not even trying to hide that he thinks he is better than the other animals.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that power is a very dangerous thing to have. Napoleon changed from a regular pig who wanted a rebellion into a scary leader who acted like Mr. Jones. The theme of power corrupting is seen from the start when they make the rules to the end when the rules are all changed to help the pigs get what they want. It is sad because the animals worked so hard just to end up back where they started with a new boss who was just as mean as the old one. This proves that having too much power makes people do bad stuff.

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, the dream of a fair society where all animals are equal quickly turns into a nightmare. The most important theme in the book is how absolute power corrupts those who lead. At the start, the animals want to escape the cruelty of Mr. Jones, but by the end, their new leaders are just as bad. Through the character of Napoleon, Orwell shows that when leaders have too much control without any rules to stop them, they will eventually become the very thing they fought against.

At the beginning of the novel, the animals are united by Old Major's vision of a world without humans. After the rebellion, they establish the Seven Commandments, the most important being, 'All animals are equal.' This shows their original goal was fairness and shared work. Napoleon starts as a quiet leader, but he quickly begins to take more than his share. For example, when the milk and apples go missing, the pigs claim they need them for their 'brainwork.' Squealer explains that 'it is for your sake that we drink that milk and eat those apples,' which is the first sign that the pigs think they are better than the others.

As the story progresses, Napoleon's greed for power grows, and he uses violence to keep it. He uses his pack of dogs to chase Snowball away, which gives him total control over the farm. This change in Napoleon shows how he moves from a revolutionary to a dictator. He stops having meetings and starts making all the decisions himself. He also starts changing the rules to fit his behavior. When the pigs move into the farmhouse, the commandment about beds is changed to say, 'No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.' This shows how Napoleon uses his power to rewrite history and justify his special treatment.

By the end of the novel, Napoleon's corruption is complete, and he is no longer recognizable as the pig who fought in the rebellion. He begins walking on two legs and carrying a whip, which were things the animals hated about humans. The Seven Commandments are erased and replaced with a single sentence: 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.' This quote is the ultimate proof of how power has ruined the original idea of Animalism. Napoleon doesn't even pretend to care about the other animals anymore; he only cares about his own status and comfort.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that power is a dangerous thing that can easily lead to corruption. Napoleon's journey from a fellow rebel to a cruel tyrant proves that the desire for control can destroy even the best intentions. By the time the pigs are sitting at the table with the humans, the other animals realize they can't tell the difference between them. Orwell's message is clear: without checks and balances, any revolution can end up replacing one dictator with another.

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, the pigs use language as a powerful weapon to maintain control over the other animals. At first, the animals use words to share a dream of equality, but soon the pigs realize they can use language to rewrite history and justify their own selfish actions. By looking at how the Seven Commandments change and how Squealer manipulates the truth, it is clear that whoever controls the language controls the people.

At the start of the rebellion, language is used to unite the farm. Snowball and Napoleon take Old Major's ideas and turn them into Animalism, which is simplified into the Seven Commandments. These rules were supposed to be unalterable laws for the animals to live by forever. However, even early on, Squealer starts using tricky language to explain why the pigs need the best food. When the milk and apples disappear, Squealer tells the others, "It is for your sake that we drink that milk and eat those apples." This shows how the pigs use science and the fear of Jones's return to make their greed sound like a sacrifice.

Squealer is the main character who shows how language is abused. He is described as a pig who could "turn black into white." As the story goes on, he changes from just being a spokesperson to a professional liar. When the pigs start breaking the rules, like sleeping in beds, the animals are confused because they remember a rule against it. Squealer changes their memory by adding words to the wall. He explains that the rule was actually "No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets." By adding those two words, he makes the pigs' behavior seem okay, and the other animals are too confused to argue.

Near the end of the book, the manipulation of language becomes even more extreme. The pigs stop caring about the original rules entirely and begin to use language to create a new, unfair reality. The most famous example is when the Seven Commandments are replaced by a single phrase: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." This is a paradox that makes no sense, but it allows the pigs to keep their power while still pretending to follow the rules of the rebellion. By this point, the pigs have used language to completely erase the original goals of the rebellion.

In conclusion, Animal Farm shows that language is one of the most effective tools for a dictator. From the first speeches of Old Major to the final rewritten commandment, the pigs use words to hide the truth and keep the other animals under their thumb. Squealer’s role as the brain of the operation proves that physical strength isn't the only way to lead; words can be just as dangerous. Orwell uses this theme to warn readers that if people don't pay attention to how language is used, they can easily lose their freedom.
